title: The Arabian Horse
summary: Where the Arabian horse came from, how desert life and Bedouin care shaped its body and gentle nature, and why its endurance and bloodlines are still valued today.
poll: The Arabian horse is the most important animal in the history of the Arabian Peninsula.

versions.title: Arabian Horses
versions.text:
Look at that horse! Its head is small. Its tail is up high. It is an Arabian horse.

This horse is a breed. A breed is one kind of horse. This breed is very old. It came from Arabia. Now that land is Saudi Arabia and the lands near it.

Long ago, the Bedouin lived in the desert. They kept these horses. The desert is hot. It is dry. Food was hard to find. So the horses grew tough.

This horse has big eyes. It has wide nostrils. They help it take in air. Its back is short. Its legs are strong. Its skin is dark. Dark skin helps in the hot sun.

The Bedouin loved their mares. A mare is a girl horse. Some mares slept in the tent! So the horses grew kind. They grew calm.

These horses can run far. They win long races. Lots of breeds have some of their blood. In Saudi Arabia, a big farm near Riyadh keeps them safe.

versions.title: The Arabian Horse: Built for the Desert
versions.text:
Imagine a horse with a small, curved face, large dark eyes, and a tail that lifts like a flag as it trots across the sand. This is an Arabian horse. It is one of the oldest horse breeds in the world.

The breed began in the Arabian Peninsula, the land that today includes Saudi Arabia and its neighbors. For thousands of years, the Bedouin raised these horses. The Bedouin are people who traveled across the desert with their animals. Life in the desert was hard. Days were burning hot, and nights could be cold. Food and water were scarce. Only the toughest horses survived, so the breed slowly became strong and hardy.

This horse is easy to spot. Seen from the side, its face has a curved, or dished, profile. It has large eyes, wide nostrils that draw in plenty of air, and an arched neck. Many Arabians have one fewer rib than other horses. This gives them a short, strong back. Under the coat, the skin is black, which protects the horse from the strong sun.

The Bedouin valued their mares, or female horses, most of all. On cold nights, a favorite mare might even sleep inside the family tent. Living so close to people helped the horses become gentle and loyal.

These horses are famous for their endurance, which means they can keep going for a very long time. They have the stamina to win races that last a whole day. Many breeds today, such as the Thoroughbred, have an Arabian ancestor in their family tree. In Saudi Arabia, a special center near Riyadh works to protect the breed.

versions.title: The Arabian Horse: A Desert Treasure
versions.text:
Imagine a horse with a delicate, curved face, large expressive eyes, and a tail that rises like a banner as it glides effortlessly across the sand. This is the Arabian horse, one of the most ancient and admired horse breeds on Earth, and its story is closely connected to the history of the Arabian Peninsula.

The breed developed in the region that today includes Saudi Arabia and its neighboring countries. For thousands of years, the Bedouin, communities who migrated across the desert with their herds, raised and protected these horses. Desert conditions were extremely demanding. Days were scorching, nights could be bitterly cold, and food and water were scarce. Because only the hardiest animals survived, the breed gradually became remarkably resilient over countless generations.

The Arabian horse possesses several distinctive physical characteristics. Viewed from the side, its face has a gently concave, or dished, profile. It has large eyes, wide nostrils that draw in abundant air during a lengthy gallop, and an elegantly arched neck. Many Arabians have one fewer rib than most other horses, which produces a compact, powerful back. Beneath the coat, the skin is black. This dark pigment shields the animal from intense desert sunlight.

The Bedouin valued their mares above all others, and families carefully memorized each mare's lineage, meaning her mother, grandmother, and earlier ancestors. On frigid nights, a treasured mare might even shelter inside the family tent. Because they lived so intimately with people, the horses became gentle, intelligent, and exceptionally loyal.

Arabian horses are celebrated for their endurance, the capacity to continue for an extraordinarily long time without exhaustion. This stamina enables them to dominate competitions covering more than one hundred kilometers. Numerous modern breeds, including the speedy Thoroughbred, are descendants of Arabian horses brought to Europe several centuries ago. In Saudi Arabia, a dedicated center near Riyadh works to preserve the breed for future generations.
